title: ‘Makes very little economic sense’: Ex-Trump energy secretary warns Trump against diesel export ban | CNN Business
text:
Source: CNN

President Donald Trump says hewants to banAmerica’s diesel exports, but his former energy secretary tells CNN this is a “bad idea” that will backfire.

“It’s one of those ideas that sounds good on the surface, but when you dig into it, it makes very little economic sense,” said Dan Brouillette, who served in Trump’s Cabinet from 2019 to 2021.

Trump has faced intensifying calls from within his own party to do something to slashsky-high prices for diesel, the workhorse fuel that powers trains, trucks, tractors and construction vehicles.

Echoing whatexperts have told CNN, Trump’s former energy secretary warnedthat choking off US diesel exports will encourage refiners to pull back on how much oil they process into gasoline, diesel andjet fuel.

“Diesel comes from the same barrel of oil that gasoline does. So when you shut down diesel refining, you also shut down gasoline refining, which constrains the market, potentially raising the price of gasoline as well as diesel,” said Brouillette, now a distinguished visiting fellow at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy.

Even Trump’s current energy secretary, Chris Wright, is pouring cold water on the proposal.

“The blunt tool of banning diesel exports definitely doesn’t work,” Wright said at an event in New York on Wednesday, according toReuters.

In other words, a diesel export ban could exacerbatewhat is already on track to be thebiggest annual percentage increase for diesel prices on record.

In the short run, researchers say blocking the 1.5 million barrels of diesel that leave the United States daily could cause diesel prices to tumble – especially along the Gulf Coast and the Midwest, where many US refineries are located.

But that excess diesel would likely be trapped in those areas because, as Brouillette notes, the United States does not have enough pipelines to transport the fuel to the East Coast and West Coast.

“It’s a bad idea. It’s not something you want to impose,” Brouillette said of the proposed export ban.

In the longer run, a US export ban risks incurring a chilling effect on foreign investment, he said. This would undermine the Trump administration’s goal of ramping up US refining capacity by expanding existing refineries, or evenbuilding the first major new refinery since 1977.

“You’re sending a really poor investment signal to those who would invest in the United States to develop this infrastructure,” Brouillette said. “If they can’t count on you to be there, they’re not going to invest their money here.”

Instead of banning US energy from getting sold overseas, Brouillette said the Trump administration should focus on building out energy infrastructure and oil production. This would mean providing tax and environmental incentives as well as ending the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war.

A White House official told CNN on Monday that the Trump administration was not considering an export ban or even export restrictions, pointing to comments from Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.

But on Tuesday, Trump sang a very different tune: He indicated he’s pushed internally for a ban on US diesel exports, when asked about GOP Sen. Chuck Grassley and others calling for such a move.

“I’ve said, ‘Let’s not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel,’” Trump told reporters.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Tuesday confirmed the administration is “examining” whether a full or partial export ban is “feasible.”

The oil industry, which typically supports the Trump administration, has blasted the talk of an export ban.

“We understand the administration is looking at every option to deliver relief, but restrictingUS energy exports would only compound the problem — exacerbating refining challenges and ultimately hurting consumers,” Mike Sommers, the president and CEO of the trade association American Petroleum Institute, said in a statement Tuesday.

Brouillette said that if he were still in the Trump administration he would try to talk the president out of an export ban.

“I would argue against the proposal, as I think many have inside of the White House,” he said. “But look, the ultimate decision maker is the president of the United States. The Cabinet is not elected. The president is, and he’s elected by the American people to make these decisions and it’s his right to make them.”
